Males variable in body colour but with oblique black streak through eye and large scales on side with dark margins, usually white face, multi coloured back and olive sides. Females can be either plain brown or bright yellow, brown form has small yellow spot mid back at base of dorsal. Juveniles brown with thin white lines radiating from eye and pair of thin white bands on body, each with a yellow spot at the top at base of dorsal fin. Large mouth can be rapidly everted to suck in passing prey. Highly similar E. brevis, from SE Asia, lacks black stripe through eye of colourful male.

Three flat spines on the opercles, a plain-coloured body that lacks spots or stripes, and a black patch around the anus. It inhabits caves but is also inquisitive and will move out to approach divers.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Pale grey/whitish with close set orange/brown spots, a straight rear edge on tail fin and a white tail margin. Length to 40 cm.

Three paired black saddles where dorsal fin joins the back, with pale strip below. Polygonal brown spots on body and high spiny dorsal fin, similar to E. maculatus (Highfin Grouper), which lacks paired black saddles on back. Length to 33 cm.
Dark grey body covered in a combination of small and large white spots, and smaller light grey spots. Large fleshy upper jaw and bulbous eyes. Length to 76 cm.

Large grouper, five alternating pairs of broken light and dark bars, orange-brown spots evenly scattered over body. Juveniles have similar markings but, fewer and relatively larger spots. Juveniles found in mangroves and estuaries.. E. malabaricus (Blackspotted Grouper) is covered with small black spots. Length to 120 cm.

Light grey grouper with an even scattering of black spots across body and fins, and a more or less distinct, irregular pattern of lighter grey blotches, often with dark patch midway along back below dorsal fin. Length to 49 cm.

photos.location: Manowar Island, Gulf of Carpentaria, Australia

description: Pale bluish-grey with even covering of small black spots, black marks on upper and lower lip. Yellow tint to fins and a black vertical bar near end of tail that fades with age, and blue becomes more grey. Length to 122 cm.

Body markings of oblique bars over back and white spots on face can all be rapidly switched to jet black or all-white. Individuals on offshore reefs often light while juveniles in estuaries are dark. Six oblique bars are almost always present in upper half of the body, the last of which consisting of or containing a dark rounded patch at upper tail base. Now totally protected after heavy fishing pressure greatly reduced population numbers last century.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

photos.location: Solitary Islands, New South Wales, Australia
Coffs Harbour, New South Wales, Australia
Solitary Islands, New South Wales, Australia

Sub adult. Lord Howe Is, NSW

description: Black and white tipped spiny dorsal fin, and red cap over head. Body colour and bars can change almost instantaneously from white or pale pink to bright red, though bars usually distinguishable. Length to 40 cm.

Yellowish-brown background with pattern of large dark blotches down side. Black markings on tail base and back are distinctive, and not as rounded as on E. polyphekadion (Camouflage Grouper). Dense covering of small dark and light spots. Juveniles found over seagrass beds. Length to 120 cm.

Similar to other groupers and rockcods with brown polygon markings such as E. merra (Birdwire Rockcod) and E. quoyanus (Longfin Rockcod), but with small white spots forming hexagonal chicken-wire pattern and 6 saddles composed of darker spots along upper back and dark patch behind eye. Length to 28 cm.

Heavy body, olive to reddish brown colouration with irregular white and brown spots and blotches, and a reddish brown stripe from snout through eye on to cheek. Red margin on fins and white tips on dorsal spines.

Distinguishable by it\'s large size. Mottled olive-brown colouration covering body and fins, often with marginal yellow-green tints, small black spots and grey green patches; juveniles with irregular black and yellow markings. Largest fish on coral reefs, growing to 300 kg. Now absent from nearly all fished reefs. Length to 270 cm.

Brown with darker polygonal pattern and high spiny dorsal fin similar to E. bilobatus (Frostback Rockcod), but with two white saddles in front of, and midway along, dorsal fin, each followed by a broad diffuse dusky patch. Younger adults with yellow fin margins. Juveniles dark brown/black with white blotches over body. Length to 62cm.
Five dark broken bars extend obliquely across body, similar to E. coioides (Goldspotted Rockcod), but with darker body, and black rather than orange/brown spots. Length to 240 cm.

Olive to dark grey, sometimes becoming pale on lower body, breast yellowish, irregular pale blotches on head and body, usually arranged in vertical series, broad, black outer margins on fins, and a yellow stripe along the top of the spiny dorsal fin. Solitary and territorial.
Honeycomb pattern of orangish brown blotches on a pale background. Distinguished from other honeycombed brown groupers and rockcods by large black spot midway along back. Length to 33 cm.

Small grouper with honeycomb pattern, highly variable and with no consistently distinctive features. Similarly-marked E. macrospilos (Snubnose Grouper) has broad white margin on tail, and E. quoyanus (Longfin Rockcod) has rounded black tail margin and larger, less numerous spots on snout. Very common within its range. Length to 31 cm.

Dark body, juveniles with white spots which darken and become smaller and more numerous with age, coalescing into scribbles on the rear of the body. Often with large pale blotches superimposed over white spotted pattern. Tail, dorsal and anal fin with black and white margin, tail fin rounded. Length to 40 cm.

Appearance varies considerably with age, and difficult to distinguish from a few other Epinephelus species. Characteristics that best distinguish it include the dense circular (rather than hexagonal) dark spots over the lower portion of the body and head, but not on the upper portion (except smaller individuals, which can have the fine spots all over). The dark blotch on the top of the tale base is also usually black, or at least much darker than other dark blotches along the back.

Small grouper with honeycomb pattern, very similar to E. merra (Birdwire Rockcod) but with polygonal spots on snout less numerous and larger (two spots between eye and upper lip), dark tailfin margin, and light and dark bars under lower jaw. Length to 31 cm.

photos.location: Smith Is, Great Barrier Reef, QLD

description: Deep body with five dark bands, yellowish tips on dorsal fin, pectoral fins with black patch at base.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Honeycomb pattern of brown polygonal markings with black spots clustering into four patches on back and above tail base, spots diminishing in size on snout. Similar E. bilobatus (Frostback Rockcod) has larger polygonal markings. Length to 35 cm.

Dark reddish-brown spots on banded, grey body, similar to E. coioides (Goldspotted Rockcod) but with densely spotted pectoral fin, and 1-3 dark blotches at dorsal fin base (but these often hidden within dark bars). Length to 75cm.

photos.photographer: Eric Keung; 114°E Hong Kong Reef Fish Survey
Ryan Cheng; 114°E Hong Kong Reef Fish Survey
Silvy Pun; 114°E Hong Kong Reef Fish Survey

description: Large, pale body with dark oval spots aligned in rows, dark streaks radiating from eye, and numerous small dark flecks all over body. Can adjust intensity of markings. Curious, approaching and following divers. Length to 200 cm.

photos.location: Comorant Passage, Great Barrier Reef, Australia

description: Fine golden-brown spots aligned in narrow rows on body and scattered on head, orange stripe above rear upper jaw in corner of mouth, fins with yellow margin. Subtropical eastern Australia, sometimes locally abundant. Length to 61 cm.

photos.location: Port Stephens, New South Wales, Australia

description: Demersal, non-migratory scavenger endemic to the Chilean coast. Individuals can grow to 93cm, and have been found at depths of 10-600m. Body is elongate, and the head and mouth are small with three pairs of barbels. Recently, its geographic distribution was reclassified to span as far north as the city of Arica in Chile, formerly thought to extend only from Valparaiso to Talcahuano.
Distinguished by its 7-9 strong rounded ribs. The colour is usually a light purple on the exterior and dark purple inside. Adults are good swimmers and generally occur in groups.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Mottled olive-green upper shell with streaks on plates, low body, small head with upper jaw projecting to form parrot-like beak, four large plates along side of shell, three scales behind eye. Harvested in large numbers last century for manufacture of tortoiseshell goods.

commercial_uses: Collected for decorative or ornamental purposes

description: Distinctive white eye that contrasts noticeably with the dark body. The species is moderately common on coastal reefs in New South Wales, where cohabiting pairs are sometimes found associated with particular caves. Black reef leatherjackets are restricted to deep water around the southern and southwestern coasts.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Numerous small brown spots across the body and bright blue colouration on the tail of the male. This species is not often seen because of its secretive habits.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Chickenwire-like network of patches on the side. Uncommon around the mainland, it rarely moves far from caves.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Distinctive and colourful arrangement of yellows, oranges and blues on the sides of a rounded body. As they age the oranges darken to black, the blues become paler and the body elongates. The smallest juveniles are common under large jellyfish in offshore waters, settling onto reefs in estuaries and sheltered bays. Adults are occasionally seen in diveable depths but are mainly confined to deep water.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

photos.location: in Catostylus mosaicus! St Leonards, Vic

description: Spines think and blunt, often encrusted. Usually found between or under rocks.
Covered with small white spots, large rounded pectoral fins, and a dense fringe of tassels right around head.

Quite similar to Castelnau’s wrasse, but has a more elongate body with the light-coloured belly abruptly darkening above, and with darker stripes down the sides. The two species also have similar swimming styles, moving in short bursts up from the bottom. When resting, the snakeskin wrasse lies on its side with head turned at an angle.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Small elongate shell with fine wavy brown lines on a pale background. It is most frequently observed at night when moving over plant blades while grazing on diatoms and other microscopic particles.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Typical dumpling squid body shape with iridescent green-yellow colouration and a covering of fine black spots. It remains hidden under sand during the day and is therefore generally seen only by divers on night dives.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Small spider crab that grows algae on its carapace as camoflage.
Stout torpedo-shaped, silver body, dark blue upper back, and patch of wavy mackerel-like markings on upper rear body.

Three dark spots along anal fin base, dorsal fin dark but may be pale centrally in females. Both E. afelei and E. punctulata have dark spots on caudal fin, a black anal fin, and dark chromatophores along the pectoral fin base, however caudal fin spots are small and set close together on rays, and fin membrane is dark in E. afelei. Scale edges are not dark in E. afelei, as seen in E. punctulata.

Part of the Eviota guttata species complex including E. teresae, E. guttata, and E. taeiae. Confirmed occurrence in the Society Islands and Tuamotus, French Polynesia; records outside of these areas are not genetically confirmed. Lacks a red interorbital spot which is seen in all other described members of the species complex. Eyes exhibit four white or gold spokes extending out from pupil, with no mottling over the iris. Red stripe behind the eye is partly connected to a large red spot behind each eye, whereas this stripe is separate in E. teresae and E. guttata.

Small, translucent reddish goby, internal gold stripes from snout along body, white stripe from pectoral fin along belly. Differs from other Eviota species in that it often hovers a small distance above the substrata. Australian records of the very similar E. pellucida are believed to be mis-identifications of this species.

Body translucent and overlaid by spindle-shaped pattern from red pigmentation of scale-pocket tissue. A midline yellow-white stripe extends along dorsal vertebral column. Lateral abdominal wall black with a dorsal yellow white stripe extending posterioirly from upper iris. Row of 6 small evenly spaced white spots from pectoral fin base to end of the black abdominal area. Upper head, snout, and iris reddish orange with yellow stripes. Rays and spines of fins pinkish with clear membranes. Described by Greenfield et al. (2024) from New Caledonia, pictured here in Vanuatu.

Two reddish stripes from snout to tail separated by a white stripe, with another short white stripe over head between eyes. Darker patch on lower tail base, and sometimes also small black spot in front of pectoral fin. Hovers in small groups above branching corals.

Dorsal side of eye exhibits short white bar next to interorbital area. A two-part black spot over the caudal peduncle, underlaid by a yellow blotch. Distinguished from similar species E. oculineata by having entire iris dark reddish and pupil surrounded by a white ring, and dorsal white line not visible from lateral view. E. oculineata has two horizontal stripes against red background of the iris; one yellow, passing through upper pupil margin, and the other white through the lower margin. Known only from Fiji and Tonga, whereas E. oculineata is far more widespread.

Part of a species complex including E. teresae, E. albolineata, and E. taeiae. Records of E. guttata outside of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman may be other species within the complex, based on variable coloration. E. guttata presents with an interorbital red spot which is distinctly disconnected to two larger red spots behind the eyes, which are connected in E. taeiae. The interorbital spot is absent in E. albolineata. Eyes exhibit thin white or gold spokes extending out from pupil, with occaisional mottling over the iris. Red stripe behind the eye is incomplete, diferentiating E. guttata from E. albolineata which exhibits a complete red stripe. Reddish rectangular blocks on the ventral side of the body are wider than they are tall.

Large black spot on tail base and 2 distinct dark spots on pectoral fin base, sometimes with additional smaller spots around these. Body may be green, red or brown, and broken by narrow white bars. Distinguishing from very similar E. distigma (Twospot Eviota) in the field problematic.

Irregular 'W' shaped dark mark on upper body, above and just posterior to pectoral fin base. Known from Seychelles and Mauritius, Western Australia and Great Barrier Reef, Japan, Palau, Micronesia, through Polynesia to French Polynesia and Pitcairn Islands.

Translucent body covered with red and white specks, alternating red and white bands across back, pair of black occipital spots on back above pectoral fins, although these can be very difficult to see (likely able to be 'switched off'), and densely spotted yellow outer eye. Squarish red blotches on belly separated by white. Pair of orange/red v-shaped patches often outlined in black between the eyes and the sometimes present occipital spot. Very similar to the Eviota guttata species complex, can be differentiated by the shape of red patches behind and between eyes.
Broad reddish stripe on body becoming black at tail base. White stripe between eyes and along upper edge of red body stripe to tail base where it curves downwards.
Pectoral fin base with two reddish vertically aligned spots, body with 4-5 ventral midline dark bars. Spinous dorsal fin with pale basal area and darker outer portion.

Translucent body, red stripe along spine with dashes along upper margin and white blotches along underside. Additional row of white spots over belly only. Distinctive red line running from tip of lower jaw, under the eye, and across the cheek. Dark spot at top of pectoral fin base and at caudal fin base below midline may be lacking or absent in live specimens. Similar species E. spilota (Shoulderspot Eviota) may be distinguished by presence of dark spot at pectoral fin base.

Both E. afelei and E. punctulata have dark spots on caudal fin, a black anal fin, and dark chromatophores along the pectoral fin base, however caudal fin spots are well spaced and fin membrane is clear in E. punctulata. No obvious dark spot over caudal fin base. Scale edges are dark.
Five postanal dark body bars, rounded dark postocular spots, and small dark spot over base of caudfal fin.

Well-defined reddish bands on male, and spot on pectoral fin base. Female with less distinctive bands. Similar E. hoesei (Doug's Eviota) and E. distigma (Distigma Eviota) lack well-defined bands, and have at least 2 spots on pectoral fin base.
editor_name: RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Semi-translucent with small red spots on the body, internal white stripe above vertebral column interrupted by red dashes, six black bars on upper iris, orange-red patch on operculum, orange-red short stripes and spots on head.
Translucent with dark, almost black, centre stripe with white dashes. Small, white-edged black spot on tail base, and orange stripes from snout to eyes. Found in loose groups on coral heads.
Small, plain translucent body with a pair of black spots on back, behind head, which can be 'switched off'. Red and gold eye with black spots on outer eye.
editor_name: RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Part of the 'Eviota bifasciata' species complex, containing six genetic lineages in the coral triangle. E. cf. bifasciata refers to a few genetically distinct lineages each with slightly different morphologies. The specimen pictured here from Vanuatu is morphologically similar to eastern Indonesian and Palauan clades of E. cf. bifasciata.
Undescribed clade within the Eviota punctulata complex, along with Eviota tigrina, Eviota maculosa, and an additional undescribed clade from Samoa.

Closest to Eviota sigillata in morphology, however local to Tonga and Fiji (may be found elsewhere). Distinct from E. sigillata in having a long silver-white line beneath the eye extending from in front of the pupil across the cheek to the posterior edge of the pre-operculum. This line is absent in E. sigillata elsewhere (Greenfield and Winterbottom, 2016).

Part of the Eviota zebrina species complex which includes eight described closely-related species, and likely more undescribed species in the Pacific. While E. zebrina is restricted to the Indian Ocean, the species pictured here from Vanuatu is likely an undescribed species within the complex, most closely resembling E. zebrina (Tornabene et al. 2021). 

Like some other species within the complex, the pictured specimens exhibit a red stripe through the centre of the iris, which is lacking in E. pseudozebrina described from Fiji. A light bar crosses above and below the pupil, topped by a red bar which is broken up by irregular light areas. A distinct reddish 'A' shaped blotch is seen immediately behind each eye, and naris are long and reddish brown. Lacks large red and yellow blotches on the caudal peduncle, seen E. zebrina and others within the complex.
Dark spot at uppermost border of pectoral fin base distinguishes this species from Eviota prasites, which lacks this marking in live specimens.

Mottled cream and brown pattern, reddish cheek, round cream spots on belly contrast with brown abdominal patch, ladder-like series of reddish bars down back. Larger individuals have dark scale edges and a lightly banded tail fin.
editor_name: RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Originally described from Nuusafee Island, Samoa, this species is a part of the Eviota guttata complex including E. guttata, E. teresae, and E. albolineata. Body with a series of taller than wide red rectangular blocks separated by yellow or white bars less than pupil diameter. Iris is red with gold spokes extending out from pupil and occaisional mottling. Red interorbital spot is connected to two larger spots behind each eye, while these are distinctly separate in E. teresae and E. guttata. Red stripe extending behind each eye is partially complete, however is incomplete in E. guttata and E. teresae.

Part of the Eviota guttata species complex including E. albolineata, E. guttata, and E. taeiae. Known to occur in Fiji, and individuals from other locations in the Coral Triangle very closely resemble the species but have not been genetically verified. Red stripe behind the eye is incomplete, and interorbital red spot is distinctly separate from a larger red spot behind each eye. Eyes exhibit a gold ring around the pupil, with no prominant spokes. The lower portion of the red rectangular blocks on the ventral side of the body are half the width of the top, and separated by white/yellow bars wider than the pupil diameter.

Translucent body with red stripe along spine, with white dashes along the upper margin, white spots on a red belly, short red ladder like stripes on back, and white spots and dashes on head. Often black spot on tail base and pair of red lines on snout. Similar E. prasites (Hairfin Eviota) has more red and lacks black tail base spot.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Relatively large with a high arched back. White background colouration with a dense covering of dark brown to black spots on head often grading to orange/pink spots at rear. Sits motionless on branched corals, spot pattern blending in with the coral polyps, but retreats quickly when approached.

First 3-4 spines of first dorsal fin elongate and/or filamentous, rows of white spots and mid-lateral row of double brown spots on body, larger faint spots/blotches on median fins. Solitary on sand near reef.

High rounded head profile, stout body with mottled brown colouring, and small white spots, faint light saddles on back, red spots and streaks on cheek and fins, and elongated rays on first dorsal fin. Found on sand/silt in sheltered or estuarine habitats.

Numerous thin white stripes running vertically across the lower half of the body behind the pectoral fins. Other features are a relatively flattened head, a long anal fin with the tip nearly reaching the tail fin, and black blotches on the side of the body.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: White body with black rhinophores. The Orange cerata have black tips. Eats the eggs of other heterobranchs.

Small species with a short snout and a body that is either dark silver or cream with about 15 broken bands. Leafy appendages on back and a yellow/orange patch on cheek. Most often seen resting on rubble or coarse sand.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

photos.location: Port Stephens, New South Wales, Australia
Port Stephens, New South Wales, Australia

description: Dark spiny dorsal fin egde. Found in large schools around branching corals in sheltered, lagoonal environments.

Relatively large body, oblique bands on cheek, regular, widely spaced blue-black bands on body. Juveniles and sub-adults have dermal appendages behind head and along body. Occasionally observed resting on rubble bottom in deep embayments. Length to 30 cm.

photos.location: Port Stephens, New South Wales, Australia
Port Stephens, New South Wales, Australia
Port Stephens, New South Wales, Australia

description: A gastropod with a flattened, oval based conical shell, with a small hole in the peak. Purplish bands radiate out from the hole in the shell, the shell is often encrusted with algae and barnacles. The animal itself has a brown and white flecked body, and a reddish head with two long antennae and a thick short trunk like mouth, the tips these are yellow or cream.
Low, flattened conical shell with an opening in the peak, and a mantle the covers entire shell with a small hole in top.

Long, thin, whip-like body, often seen held perfectly straight when swimming slowly and undulating with a snake like motion when swimming quickly. Snout extremely long and narrow and has a long tail filament. Blue lines and spots on body, lacks row of bony plates on back in front of dorsal fin as in F. petimba (Rough Flutemouth) . Long filament extending from the middle of the tail, absent in Aulostomus chinensis (Trumpetfish).

photos.location: Solitary Islands, New South Wales, Australia

description: Pale crinoid with about 10 arms.

Recognisable by size and an extremely long tailfin. Males are very colourful with a pink tinge to the body, blue markings on the fins and side of the head, and yellow lips. Females have a drab body except for blue wavy lines on the head and fine blue spots on the fins.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Distinct long snout, yellow body and black spot on anal fin. Head black on top and white on bottom. Snout shorter than F. longirostris (Longnose Butterflyfish) which also has black spots on the white breast.

Distinct long nose, yellow body with a black and white head, and black ocellus on anal fin. Numerous small black spots on breast and more elongated snout distinguishes it from F. flavissimus (Forceps fish). Also less common.
In breeding males body is yellow and head is black. Females and non-breeding males white anteriorly, white or yellow posteriorly, and black stripe along lateral line only extends to mid-body.

photos.location: Spawning. Poor Knights Is, New Zealand
Spawning. Poor Knights Is, New Zealand

description: Body white through grey-brown to black (spawning males are black). Black stripe from above the eye to the tail (not visible in black specimens). Endemic to New Zealand, but introduced to Victoria's Port Phillip Bay (e.g. Geelong area), presumably via ships' ballast water. Darker specimens could be confused with F varium, but the latter lacks the stripe, is of a more blotchy appearance and has a yellow eye. F varium is another New Zealand endemic which has also made its way to Australia, but this time to Hobart, Tasmania.

photos.location: Spawning. Poor Knights Is, New Zealand

description: Body yellow with broad, black stripe extending along upper side of body. Mouth is strongly angled upward.

Large triplefin with mottled brown, green and pink body and a first dorsal fin with six to seven spines in contrast to the three of most other local species in the family. Males are brighter than females and have bluish tips to the fins. Spawning males are black but may retain the bluish tips to the fins. F varium has a more yellowish eye compared to the similar F lapillum. The latter normally has a distinctive black stripe, but spawning males also turn black, becoming hard to distinguish from F varium spawning males. F varium has been introduced to Tasmania from New Zealand. Another introduced, but uncommon triplefin, the estuarine threefin Grahamina gymnota, is also found on the same reefs in the Derwent Estuary. That species differs from the many-rayed threefin in having a more bulbous head and the first spine in the first dorsal fin longer than the next few spines, rather than shorter.

photos.location: Lizard Island, Great Barrier Reef, Australia
Lizard Island, Great Barrier Reef, Australia

description: Fromia polypora is one of the most common species of seastar observed on southeastern Australian reefs with heavy wave exposure. It is usually quite easy to see due to its long, bright orange arms which are covered in small, black papulae. Like most conspicuous, temperate seastar species, its diet consists mainly of sedentary invertebrates such as sponges and ascidians.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

photos.location: With Petricia vernicina, left. Port Macquarie, NSW

description: Pale translucent body, fine brown lines on back, one extending on to the first dorsal fin, visible on close inspection, fine spots over body tending to blotches and dashes on head. Sometimes with two black spots on first dorsal fin. Found on sand patches near reefs.

Elongate first dorsal spine, especially in males, translucent body with, internal stripe of alternating black and white dashes, ending in a black spot on tail base, belly with black and white blotches, and body covered in yellow spots. Found on sand and rubble patches near reefs.

Semi-translucent pale body with dark speckling, and first dorsal fin with a dark patch that can vary from olive to dark grey. Similar F. signipinnis (Flasher Sandgoby) has red colour in eye and on 1st dorsal fin. Found on sand patches near reefs.

Translucent body covered in fine white and brown spots, short brown bars on back below dorsal fins, first dorsal fin with faint white margin and black spot half way up leading edge. Found on sand patches near reefs.
Semi-translucent. Body, head and fins with many small yellow-orangish spots dotted with dark brown. Black spot (may be tipped with white) at top of first dorsal fin is distinctive.

Pale, translucent body covered in brown and white spots, large dark reddish flag-like patch on first dorsal fin, which it flicks up and down ('flashing'), and reddish eyes. Thin internal stripes of white and dark red dashes. Similar F. melacron (Blacktip Sandgoby) lacks red on fin and eyes. Found on sand patches near reefs.

resembles Pleuroploca australasia except that it is smaller, with a longer siphonal canal, and lacks the angular, nodulose shoulders on the whorls. It occurs most commonly in small aggregations on sand near seagrass along the western section of the southern coast.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Spectacular looking spindle shell with an extremely long siphonal canal.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Lacks the blue stripes seen in similar species Galathea strigosa but easily mistaken for Galathea nexa. Distinguished from G. nexa by a pointed and narrow rostrum, which is wider in G. nexa.

Males do not exceed 4cm in length, and females 3cm. Lacking blue stripes seen in similar species Galathea strigosa and has a wider rostrum and more hair on first pair of legs than Galathea dispersa (previously thought to be the conspecific).
Large, deep-bodied. Extended series of vertical bars, sometimes indistinct, on body; rounded snout, and small black eye.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Body stellate with five tapering arms, dorsal surface orange to red and granulated.
Large white nudibranch, with a \'furry\' texture on back, a tuft of gills on rear of back and two rhinopores on head.

Body is yellow to white with minute black or brown speckles and circular gills. Similar to Diaulula sandiegensis, however spots are solid rather than rings. Spots do not extend onto tubercles, as seen in Doris montereyensis.

Black stripes radiating back from eye on white central body, upper and lower body grey, dorsal fin black, yellow patch on top of head, grey tail with black spots, and elongated tips on upper and lower lobes. Similar male Genicanthus watanabei (Watanabe's Angelfish) has stripes on underside. Lacks vertical banding of males of other similarly distributed Genicanthus species, and also distinguished by presence of stripes in female. Length to 25 cm.

Male with full black vertical bars on a pale body, and on upper head down to eye level, fins with blue margins, swallow tail with yellowish tinge and orange spots on base, and black spot on breast in front of pelvic fins; female with yellow back, pale blue belly, and blue swallow tail with black upper and lower lobes. Length to 18 cm.

Males grey with black narrow vertical bands on upper body, orange-brown unmarked belly, orange tinge on back and dorsal fin, swallow tail with black spots, blue margins on orange upper and lower lobes and trailing filaments. Vertical bands less dense than on similar G. melanospilos (Swallowtail Angelfish) and absent over top of head. Females dark grey on upper body and pale on belly with blue margins on median fins and a blue arc encasing a black blotch above eye. Length to 21 cm.

Male with numerous thin black stripes on white lower body only, blue head, upper body and tail, dorsal fin with black margin. Female with pale blue body, black bars across forehead above eye, dark margins to dorsal, anal and tail fins. Length to 15 cm.

Large, mottled eel-like species that is closely related to the cods. The dorsal and anal fins are continuous with the tail, and the ventral fins lie below the head and have been reduced to probing feelers. During the day, adult rock ling remain in caves, where they are often mistaken for conger eels, while juvenile animals are observed in sheltered seagrass habitats.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Reflective silver body, black spot on dorsal fin lobe and elongate spines at the start of the dorsal fin. Concave bottom profile of the head, like in other silverbiddy species.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Rounded head, dark blue body, with random pattern of green-brown scales.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Similar in shape to the luderick, but has an overall bluish black colour with no obvious markings. It is not seen often, probably partly because it remains hidden for most of the day in caves in shallow habitats with wave surge. The related western rock blackfish Girella tephraeops, a species found from Carnarvon to Esperance, has much fewer scales along the lateral line (80-86 cf. 50-58), and a mottled appearance.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Grey body with about 10 thin dark lines down the sides. Adults occur abundantly in estuaries and on shallow coastal reefs, while juveniles are normally associated with estuarine seagrasses during the first year before moving into deeper channels nearby.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Similar shape to other Girella sp., but is easily recognised with the yellow fins and eight dagger-shaped bars down the body. It occurs abundantly in schools of 5-30 animals on shallow sheltered reefs, particularly near boulder fields.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Orange to purple, five armed sea star with a row of short spines around the edges, and a scattering of short spines and a covering of short, retractable, translucent tentacles on dorsal surface.
Dark curved band through eye and wide, horizontal dark stripes which fade with age. The dorsal fin of adults tapers to a projecting point; juveniles have six black stripes along the body.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Dark brown/gold bars on head, one passing through the eye and two more behind eye, gold spots on body, long trailing filaments on dorsal and anal fins.
editor_name: RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Dark bar through the eye, more distinct in juveniles, upper body with black spot at rear base of dorsal fin, olive-brown scales forming thin lines along body.
Distinguished by a nearly circular carapace, and legs coated in setae which appear hairy. Claws have dark tips, and carapace is typically dull red dorsally, and white ventrally.
Similar to Doriprismatica atromarginata but has a wider body and smoother mantle edge. The mantle has a dark brown to black edge.

Body is fleshy and lumpy, oval shaped with pronounced undulations on the mantle edge. The mantle edge has a broad yellowish band outlined by a narrow blue/green or black line. The gills and rhinophores are pale to darker brown. Feeds on sponges.
The mantle has an orange-brown speckled pattern. The mantle edge is a similar colour with a white submarginal band.
Highly distinctive head. It is possibly common on rubbly bottom but is rarely noticed because the shape and colour pattern provide excellent camouflage.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Bright orange with large floppy fins, however, the fish is difficult to detect because the colour seems quite dull in the near absence of red light and the animal sways like nearby kelp plants with the surge. Reef monitoring studies indicate that the population may have declined greatly over the past 20 years. Being spiked by the red velvetfish is said to cause excruciating pain, which can last for many hours.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Combination of five faint bars with narrower bars between, large dark spots often present, colour of bright yellow juveniles gradually fades with age. Mouth is more protrusible and 'rubbery' than other trevallies, made to pump food out of the sand. Forms large schools, often mixed with Carangoides fulvoguttatus (Turrum) which lacks vertical bars and has slightly more angular head. Juveniles school in front of sharks and other large fishes, and also can accompany divers.
editor_name: RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Broad gold stripe along lateral line with thin widely spaced gold lines below and darker more dense lines above, yellow blotch at rear base of dorsal fin and yellow patch at base of pectoral fin. Sometimes forms large aggregations low down over the reef.
editor_name: RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Narrow vertical bar through eye to bottom of head, profile of head steep and rounded. Markings highly variable, but tend to be less linear compared with those of G. cauerensis (Eyebar Goby). Yellow shoulder spot is not diagnostic and isn't always present. Found on sand patches near reefs.

Narrow vertical bar through eye to bottom of head. Markings highly variable, but tend to be more distinctly linear down the side compared with those of G. anjerensis (Shoulderspot Sandgoby). Shoulder spot is not diagnostic, varying between individuals, and even between sides of a single individual. Found on sand patches near reefs.

High, yellow body, small black spot at pectoral fin base, two blue bars over eye, one at back of head and one on pectoral fin base, and blue stripes along base of dorsal and anal fin. Lives amongst coral, often on openly branching corals and less shy than other coral gobies. Produces toxic mucus.
Greenish-brown body with narrow red bars on head and spots or lines on body. Very shy and cryptic, live at the base of fingers of Acropora corals.
Bright yellow body, rounded head. Lives down amongst the branches of Acropora corals. Similar to yellow form of G. spilophthalmus (Whitelined Coralgoby), but lacking the light patch along side.

Light brown body with five narrow blue bars on head, two of which passing through eye. Differs from G. quinquestrigatus (Fiveline Coralgoby) primarily by narrower, less tapered body shape. Lives at the base of fingers of Acropora corals.

Red/brown body with 5 narrow blueish-white bars on head. Differs from G. prolixus (Elongate Coralgoby) primarily in body shape, with deeper head tapering more towards tail. Live at the base of fingers of Acropora corals.

Possibly an undescribed species (Gobiodon species 1 in Allen & Erdmann 2012), although that species is only known from Brunei, Philippines and Ryuku Islands. Maze-like pattern of blue lines on the top of the head, two blue or pale lines below the eye, and finer blue lines on the operculum and pectoral fin base. Found in the branches of Acropora hard corals. Similar to, and possibly a colour variation of G. quinquestrigatus or G. prolixus.

Found deep in the branches of Acropora hard corals. Colour patterns with red stripe along back and blue bands on head and becoming less distinct down the body represents those of an undescribed species shown in Allen & Erdmann 2012 as Gobiodon species 3, although that has only been recorded in SE Asia. Also possibly a variation of similar G. histrio, G. rivulatus or G. quinquestrigatus.

Small body with a blunt rounded head. Two colour forms: the first, golden with gold eye, and the second, translucent with two black stripes along body on either side of a white stripe, with black spots on head and tail, and spotted eye. Both with a light stripe along mid side, and can both occur in the same place. Less shy than other Gobiodon species (Coralgobies), often sitting on coral surfaces in plain sight.

photos.location: Lizard Island, Great Barrier Reef, Australia

description: Dark wrasse with extended 'beak-like' snout, male with pale blue margin along pectoral fin, and lime green dorsal and anal fin; female with pale lower head and breast, dark stripe through eye, and yellow anal and tail fin. Juveniles pale with dark streak from snout through eye onto body. Differs from similar G. varius (Birdnose Wrasse) differs by location, and by bright green streak on side in males, lack of yellow tail in females, and green back in juveniles.

Distinctive long 'beak-like' snout. Males dark green with a bright green vertical bar behind pectoral fin. Females with white lower head and breast, black rear body, front upper half of body light grey with rows of black spots, red snout. Juveniles with green back, thin black stripe, white sides, and another black stripe below. Differs from the Gomphosus caeruleus (Green Birdnose Wrasse) by location, and by males having light bar, females with black rear body and juveniles having green back.

Humpbacked profile. Body with black and white oblique bars, rearmost black bar largest, extending from mid back below dorsal fin onto lower lobe of tail, small horn near eye (often red), opercular margin orange, black patch below eye, and tip of upper tail lobe black. Similar to the temperate C. vestitus (Crested Morwong), but differs by black tip on upper tail lobe, and by location. Tasman Sea islands, New Caledonia and Kermadec islands. Previously misidentified as the Hawaiian C. vittatus (Hawaiian Morwong). Length to 50 cm.

High humped shoulder with tapering body, white with broad dark to black oblique bands across face and below dorsal profile extending to caudal peduncle. Fourth spine of the dorsal fin greatly elevated, and the following spines gradually diminishing in size.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Pattern of oblique brown bands across the body, spots between the bands, and red markings on the lips, opercle edge, and pectoral and pelvic fins. It is the morwong most commonly seen by divers on the west coast, and generally lives in caves in shallow weedy areas of reef.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Humpbacked profile with black and white oblique bars on body, yellow upper tail lobe, yellow stripe below dorsal fin, and yellow patch behind eye. Similar to Cheilodactylus franscisi (Blacktip Morwong) but lacks black patch below eye, and black tip on upper tail lobe.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: White body with orange margin to mantle. Large rhinophores in proportion to body size.
White mantle with yellow to brown spots. Large purple spots around edge of mantle.
Black & white lines surrounding a central tan coloured mantle area. Purple line to the edge of the mantle. Mantle skirt undulates as the animal crawls.

photos.location: Blue Pearl Bay, Great Barrier Reef

description: Mantle is bordered with purple, which abutts a broad white region surrounding a large central portion of translucent red-orange to brown. The outer half of the white mantle portion is scattered by numerous yellow spots. Purple spots are typically larger, and are more numerous on the inner half. Dark patches and scattered white specks can also be found in the central orange portion. Rhinophore stalk is translucent, and club is dark red-brown with white specks. Gills are translucent, with dark brown lines bordering the inner and outer edges.
White body with small red / orange spots. Red rhinophores and gills and a red / orange margin to the mantle. Several similar species.

Translucent mantle with a white line running dorsally along body which ends in a Y shape. Another white line runs around the outside of the rhinophores along the body to below the gills. There are scattered purple dots and an orange border along the mantle edge.

Light coloured body, usually with a row of orange spots around the outer margin and fine orange spots on the back. Animals living in the western part of the range generally have a pink background, whereas those from Tasmania are white. The species is moderately common and is often associated with the sponge Aplysilla rosea.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Characterised by the four bands around the edge of the mantle - the outermost is white, then translucent greyish purple, then white, then yellow.
White body with nodules and black lines. Rhinophores are yellow/green, the edge and underside of the mantle is purple. The mantle skirt waves up and down as the animal crawls along.

White Body with red spots and semi-translucent yellow margin to mantle. Gills and rhinophores are white. There are several similar species in NSW, Australia including Goniobranchus loringi, Goniobranchus daphne, Goniobranchus splendidus, Goniobranchus tasmaniensus, Verconia haliclona.
Pale pink body with red / orange spots and yellow margin to mantle. Rhinophores have yellow tips
White Body with red spots and yellow margin to mantle. Gills and rhinophores are red.

White body and mantle covered in orange spots with lines around the rims of the rhinophores and gill cavities. The size and number of the spots is highly variable and appears to vary with location. This nudibranch lives in a similar habitat to Chromodoris epicuria but is slightly less common.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: White body with a network of red lines over the upper body and orange margin bordered by red spots.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: White mantle with an outer red and inner orange border. Red gills and rhinophores.

White edge to mantle and red spots on the body which central in blue patches. The mantle has a narrow yellow / orange margin. A very similar species Chromodoris thompsoni is differentiated by having the red spots in the offset in the blue patches.
Goniocidaris impressa is distinguished by the scrobicular spines which are club shaped, not pointed or flattened as in G. tubaria.

Large, serrated primary spines, which are often eroded and covered by sessile invertebrates, and platelike secondary spines, which form a corona-like structure around the base of the primary spines. The similar Goniocidaris impressa has scrobicular spines which are club shaped, not pointed or flattened as in G. tubaria.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Purple marginal plates, purple tubercles on the upper surface and rust-coloured patches. It is the most abundant seastar in seagrass beds off Perth, where it is found half-buried in sand.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Small white nudibranch with yellow / brown markings along the edge of the mantle and often a line down the centre of the mantle. The rhinophores and oral tentacles often have yellow / brown tips.

Grey-green body with a blue-edged dark mask over eye, white tail base with central black spot (can be darkened), large grey to white saddle on a black back, and sides often with slightly curved dark bars. Juvenile bright purple and similar to Pseudanthias species (Basslets), with red dorsal and anal fins and upper and lower tail margins. Length to 40 cm.

Front half blue/purple and rear half orange/yellow, black spot on front of dorsal fin and a large mouth. Usually found in small groups in caves and under ledges were it swims upside with it\'s belly aligned with the ceiling. Endemic to Brazil.

Elongate silver body, greenish on back, double lateral line, lower line departing on perpendicular angle behind pectoral fin and re-joining on tail base. Common large mackerel around reefs, difficult to distinguish from G. bicarinatus (Shark Mackerel), which also has 2 lateral lines, but has proportionally smaller eye.

High rounded body with thin yellow stripes and a blue edged black spot on upper lip. The number, length and continuity of stripes varies with age with juveniles only having two white stripes. Juveniles on coastal reefs and adults in deeper water. Usually well back in caves and under ledges during the day. Skin has toxic poison. Length to 30cm
Cream shell with numerous fine spiral ridges and a pearly interior. Because of its very large aperture, it superficially resembles a small abalone.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Large square bodied with a smooth red-brown carapace, patterns of light knobs on pincers, yellowish ridges along legs, and green eyes, deeply indented front carapace teeth and a covering of felt that extends in rows down the legs. Often found hiding in crevices and under ledges in the reef. The species feeds mainly on encrusting bryozoans, sponges and hydroids. Some authors separate it from other grapsids in the family Plagusiidae.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Body extremely elongate and pale blue, small black spot at rear of opercle, small blue line under eye. Occurs in colonies evenly spread over white sand; animals rapidly dive under sand if disturbed.

Mottled black and white pattern which, from a distance, can be mistaken for that of a fortescue; however, the two species are easily separated because the soldierfish has smooth skin with no scales. They pose a hazard to barefoot bathers because of the venomous spines. In late winter and early spring adult soldierfish leave these shallow seagrass beds to congregate in deeper water in huge concentrations, presumably for spawning. The species is quite slow growing and large soldierfish are considerably older (more than 10 years) than most other species at the same size.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: High body profile with steeply sloping head, pale silvery with a light blue sheen,, face distinctly pale and scaleless, distinctive semicircular patch on head above and behind eye, often with olive or light brown on upper sides and brown flecks on body. Length to 40 cm.
Silver-grey body with scattered black spots on sides, high body profile with steeply-sloping head, and large tail with rounded lobes.
editor_name: RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Silvery body with darker scale centres on back, pointed snout and a dark vertical bar on face through eye. Length to 45cm.
New species described in 2013. Silvery-white with large black spots on scales of back, which form rows. Black eyebrow above eye, dark bar through eye to rear of jaw.
Muddy brown to golden brown colouration with a blue iris. Indented head profile with a groove from snout below eye.

photos.location: Storms River Mouth, Eastern Cape Province, South Africa

description: White body with orange spots and an orange border around the front of the mantle. Rhinophores have orange tips and the gills have orange lines on the outer edge.
Body white to orange with scattered orange spots across entire surface. Gills form a complete circle.
Translucent pale cream body, numerous orange spots and fewer raised white pustules. The gills and rhinophores are similar to the body colour. Grows to 40 mm. Feeds on smaller nudibranchs.
Dense banding pattern distinctive, with bands much narrower than on the more slender-bodied snake eels (Ophichthidae).
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Torpedo-shaped, two-tone body, grey-blue on back and silver below. White tips on dorsal and anal fins, black tips on tail, obvious lateral line which dips down to lower body at mid body and large mouth with large teeth. Found along walls, bommies and reef passes near deep water.

Yellowish body and light grey head, with numerous darker blotches. Tail may have white margin. Localised, differing from co-occurring G. eurostus (stout moray) by light/grey rather than yellow base colour on head.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Light spots on head, usually with light patch on the upper section of lower jaw near the corner of the mouth. Otherwise variable in colour, including nearly all brown, or dark brown bars and blotches on reddish background.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

photos.location: Solitary Islands, New South Wales, Australia

description: Grey brown body with a covering of fine white spots, less dense on head and snout with a yellow tint. Lives in cracks and crevices in the reef with just the head poking out, constantly opening and closing mouth to breathe.
Colour variable, but usually with head, or at least snout, with yellow tinge. Black/brown speckles and mottling pattern, tending to dark blotches on body.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

photos.location: Colour variation, Lord Howe Is, Australia

description: Smaller individuals black with narrow white tessellated pattern. Adults with more widely spaced, mostly circular spots. Blotches are variable between individuals. Often found in holes with cleaner wrasses or shrimps.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: A medium sized moray most active at night. Base colour cream to light green with scattered dark spots, often the corners of the mouth are white.

Black patch above gill opening and bronze-coloured eye. Fine brown speckling or marbling on yellow/cream body - sometimes giving a cappuccino-like appearance. Similar to G. javanicus (giant moray) and G. porphyreus (lowfin moray) but the former with darker eye and greenish tinge to back, and the latter lacking the black gill marking.
Very large moray, uniformly olive green to brown. Inhabits holes and crevices in the reef where it sits with just its head protruding, opening and closing it's mouth to fan water over its gills.
Black around gill opening. Brown body with fine darker speckles and greenish tinge to back. Has darker eye than G. flavimarginatus (yellowmargin moray).
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Distinguished by combination of markings, eye colour and head shape. Only confirmed from Japan and Taiwan. Australian records of this species (including Australian photos shown here) are likely G. mucifer, a name recently resurrected, but not yet reflected in major taxonomic databases.

photos.location: Solitary Islands, New South Wales, Australia
Solitary Islands, New South Wales, Australia

description: Small Moray with variable colouring, from brown to bright yellow, with or without small brown spots or sometimes even a reticular pattern. Eye is blue, often with a dark bar running through the iris. Quite common but shy and rarely seen by divers.
White inside mouth. Brown body with uniform white spots.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: White with a dense covering of brown blotches, and two round, bare white spots on lower jaw. Inhabits crevices and holes in the reef where it sits with only its head protruding, opening and closing its jaws to fan water over its gills.
Creamy beige head and body with light brown blotches on body. Tail with white margin. White eye with black stripe. Often out in the open.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Dark moray with constellation of small white spots, distinctive yellow lining of mouth, head small relative to body, and less distinct teeth than most morays. Length to 180 cm.

Dense dark brown speckles on lighter brown base. G. javanicus (giant moray) and G. flavimarginatus (yellowmargin moray) have obvious black patch above/around gill opening. A temperate to sub-tropical NZ species, only occasionally seen in Australia at Tasman Sea Islands. Sometimes mistaken for G. obesus, which is rare and only known from a few specimens taken from deeper water in SE Australia and New Zealand.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Yellowish brown humped head, blending into a green body. The species generally remains concealed in crevices during the day and moves about in the open when feeding at night. A second temperate moray eel, the speckled moray Gymnothorax obesus, occurs along the New South Wales coast. This eel is easily distinguished by colour pattern, as it has numerous cream speckles scattered over a brown body. A few tropical moray eels also occasionally occur, but are rarely encountered.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

photos.location: With Enchelycore ramosa. Poor Knights Is, New Zealand
With Gymnothorax nubilus. Poor Knights Is, New Zealand

description: Narrow head with spots and yellow eye, and linked dark brown bars along body. Brown-speckled yellowish patches intervene. Fins with lighter margin.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Yellowish-brown top of head. Grey body with faint dark bars. Bars prominent on dorsal fin margin, giving dashed appearance.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: White eye with small black pupil. Light snout tip on darker grey head. Often in pairs or sharing crevice with another moray species.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Mosaic pattern over the body, similar to Enchelycore ramosa (mosaic moray) but shorter snout/smaller mouth.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Brown and white markings on face, including bars on lower jaw and broad brown stripe extending rearwards from the eye.
editor_name: extract from RD Stuart-Smith, GJ Edgar, AJ Green, IV Shaw. 2015. Tropical Marine Fishes of Australia. Reed New Holland

description: Pale with two distinct yellow stripes along body from snout, the bottom one through the eye, numerous narrower, less distinct lines over rest of body, and a dark spot on tail base (may not be present). Forms schools.

Reasonable high, silvery grey body, each scale with light pearly spot in centre, yellowish fins, and a dark tail base, sometimes displaying a rounded spot. Often forms large schools mixed with other fishes.

Slightly reddish, grey body with light spots on scale centres forming lines along body, tail dark maroon, or often showing large rounded dark spot on base. Forms large schools around coastal reefs during the day, dispersing over sand areas at night.
Silver-grey with dark scale centres forming a spotted pattern over body (more distinct on upper body), dorsal and anal fins dark. Juveniles use seagrass beds and mangroves as nurseries.

High body with a pointed snout and a straight, sloping forehead profile. Body with blue spots on scale centres, fading and becoming more scattered towards tail, and yellow fading on belly. Head with numerous blue stripes. Back ground colour may vary but most commonly yellow. Juveniles with small black spot on tail base. Forms dense aggregations on reefs and over sand.
Silvery grey body with dark scale centres, and a series of six light bars on back, fading onto lower sides. Back relatively high, with a slightly pointed snout.

Brassy on upper sides and back, silvery on belly, indistinct dark lines following scale rows on body, fins yellowish and a large round black spot on tail base extending slightly on to tail fin. Generally found of sand and rubble bottoms, less frequently over reefs, and usually on schools.

A large species with yellow eyes and a whiting-like slender body. It is only found in sheltered habitats without direct swell exposure, typically Sargassum beds or seagrass. Females are most common, and look like a larger version of Neoodax balteatus, but lacking the dark stripe down the side. Males are rare, and have bright blue lines on the face and a darker body than the green females.

White background with orange-tipped tubercles and large orange patches between tubercles. Mantle has a solid orange border, and gills and rhinophores have back speckles. Similar species Halgerda carlsoni lacks solid mantle border, and has fine orange speckles between orange-tipped tubercles rather than large orange patches.

Body white with fine network of solid orange lines and numerous orange tipped tubercles. The mantle edge is pale with a line of small orange tubercles around its circumference. The rhinophores and gills are pale with numerous brown spots. Grows to 40 mm.

White background with raised, rounded tubercles tipped in orange. Small orange specks are also scattered across the white mantle between tubercles, except around the mantle edge. Gills and rhinophores exhibit black speckles, with variable densities among individuals- some appearing wholly black, and others sparsely speckled. Similar species Halgerda aurantiomaculata lacks small orange specks across the mantle and exhibits a solid orange mantle border.

Three short spines of equal size on the front margin between the eyes. It has an almost rounded carapace, which bends at a blunt point on the front of each side, and is extremely variable in colour pattern.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Purplish body, orange and green stripes on head that extend rearward and disappear along body. Commonly seen with 2 ocelli on dorsal fin, although these are lost with age. Juveniles distinguished from H. marginatus (Dusky Wrasse) and H. melanurus (Hoeven's Wrasse) by having 3 dorsal fin ocelli and a black spot on the tail base.

Adults green with red streaks on scales aligning to make narrow red bands on sides, a large red patch on cheek, oblique green lines through eye and red scribbles behind eye. Fins with iridescent blue lines and spots, and tail fin triangular green markings in corners. Juveniles pale with a yellow top half of head, two yellow stripes along mid side, another less distinct stripe along back and three black ocelli (two on back/dorsal fin and one on tail base). Large individuals are usually found below 10m depth, while juveniles prefer shallow water such as tide pools.

Green to brown with broad tapering white stripe from face along lower body, thin broken white stripe along upper body and numerous small black spots on side. Small ocelli on rear of dorsal fin and tail base, but not always visible. It is not often noticed because of its small size and good camouflage.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Terminal phase with a blue and green mottled body, bright green cheek and patch behind pectoral fin, and a black and red blotch on mid back. Initial phase mottled red-brown with a yellow cheek and a white belly. Juveniles brown with blotchy white bands on body, white cheek and three small ocelli on dorsal fin.

Males pale green, head with pink and green squiggles and a large dark patch on upper body. Females green to mauve, fine evenly-spaced black spots aligned in rows on side, small yellow patch behind eye, pectoral fin with yellow base, pink stripe from snout through eye and a series of dark curved lines on lower side behind pectoral fin which diffuse to a faint grey area with age. Juveniles translucent green and lack ocelli of other similar green wrasses.

photos.location: Brook Is, Great Barrier Reef, QLD

description: Bright yellow body, black mark at start of dorsal fin, faint green lines on snout, andtransparent tail corners. Juveniles with two ocelli on dorsal fin and one on upper tail base. Similar golden stages of Thalassoma lutescens (Green Moon Wrasse) lack the transparent tail corners and small dorsal fin ocelli.

Bright yellow top of head and back, blue sides, pale belly and broad yellow margin on tail fin. An oblique dark yellow bar edged in blue extends above and behind the eye. Adults usually found in deeper waters, below 20m, juveniles in shallower waters where they act as cleaners to larger fish.
Red-brown body with light mottling on back, yellow lower head and blue stripes on cheek below a red eye. Juveniles mainly white with brown/black blotches over body.

Males apricot to grey-pink body with a blue-edged dark spot on back above pectoral fin, red blotch on belly overlaid with blue markings, blue markings on face and rows of blue dashes along body. Females with a small black spot on back, no blue markings and a round black spot on tail base. Juveniles grey with an iridescent blue stripe along mid body, another less distinct stripe along back and a black spot on tail base.

Male colourful with green body, black pectoral fin base, yellow/red stripe running along body from above pectoral fin, yellow patch behind gill cover at start of stripe and wavy purple lines radiating from eye. Females pale with yellow stripe from eye to tail. Juveniles pale with brown stripe and black spot on tail base.

Males green with dark blue scale centres forming a chequered pattern on sides, green head with red broken stripes, broad light bar behind pectoral fin, blue tail and yellow spot on back below start of dorsal fin. Female with vertical rectangular black streaks on scales creating a black and white chequered patter on upper sides, rectangular marks giving way to fine spots lower down the body, two yellow blotches and large black blotch on back, yellow head with pink lines and yellow dorsal and tail fins. Juveniles with mottled black and white bands, yellow blotches around head, yellow edged occulls on dorsal fin and a yellow tail.

Adults blue-grey with dark scale edges, blue scribbles on face, a blotch on rear corner of gill cover and a red eye. Initial phase pink with a white belly and a yellow head. Juveniles pale with two red stripes, and a black spot or rear corner of gill cover. Found near reefs over coarse sand and gravel. Found only around Malpelo Island.

Males green with pink/red mottling on body and lines on face, yellowish belly, black spot in centre of dorsal fin, curved pink line around a horizontal bar on cheek distinguishes this species from similarly marked species. Females olivaceous with irregular white spots on back, white belly with a broad, oblique, pink band between pelvic and anal fins, ocellus in middle of dorsal fin, and a black patch behind eye. Sub-adult males with large black patch on side.

Males green-brown with thin dark green stripes along body, bright green band on tail fin base, high body profile and pointed snout. Females and juveniles brown with darker stripes along body, two ocelli on dorsal fin, and translucent band on tail fin base. Small juveniles black with light stripes along body.

Purple, body grading to a light white/yellow tail, orange pelvic fins, often all fins orange, small black spot on the upper rear of tail base, large black spot at base of pectoral fin and fine black spots arranged in rows on side. Juveniles with black and white stripes along body, large ocellus on mid dorsal fin and a small ocellus on upper tail base.

Males green with numerous stripes along the body, broken by a series of short bars on the back, and with yellow and black pectoral fin base. Females and juveniles with fine pinstripes, two ocelli on dorsal fin (which disappear with age), and one on upper tail base. Very common. Indian Ocean populations from western Indonesia to the Maldives considered a separate species (H. chrysotaenia), with spots on the tail of males, but this is not yet reflected in global databases.

Males green with pale belly, broken red stripes along body, red lines on face, one of which curves in a circle below eye, sub-adults with dark brown streak along side. Females and juveniles brown with white dashes forming lines along body, short dark bar behind eye, pale belly with yellow blotch behind pectoral fin, and translucent spotted tail and anal fins. Ring on cheek of males distinguishes it from similarly marked species.

photos.location: Hudson Is, Great Barrier Reef, QLD
Hudson Is, Great Barrier Reef, QLD

description: Small mottled wrasse with red lines on green head, dark blotches on side, yellow markings in front of and behind pectoral fin base, followed by a red patch on a pale belly; distinguished from similar species by red stripe on green cheek that is curved in arch. Small individuals best confirmed by presence of adults, or by carefully comparing body markings.

Males blue-green with narrow vertical light streaks on each scale, a yellow blotch on fore body, followed by a broad dark band which is in turn followed by a diffuse light band. Head mildly pointed, with blue spots on upper head, lower head unmarked, and dorsal, anal and tail fins with blue spots and dashes. Females pinkish to grey with a dark stripe along body broken on fore-body and joined by an upside down triangular mark on back. Tail fin and underside yellow. Hides under sand to sleep, and shelter from danger.

Green body, pale red stripes along side that break apart and interconnect towards rear, dark stripe from snout to eye, black mark at base of pectoral fin, small black spot on upper tail base and yellow corners on tail fin. Juveniles with four white spots on side, which expand to become short vertical bars breaking the body stripes of adults.

photos.photographer: Caron Wong; 114°E Hong Kong Reef Fish Survey
Ken Kwok; 114°E Hong Kong Reef Fish Survey

description: Brown body with a series of seven light bars, narrow blue streaks on scales and blue spots on red tail, anal and dorsal fins. Usually found near areas with high concentrations of brown algae.

Green body with broken, irregular red stripes, pale belly, black spot in centre of dorsal fin. Females with green scale centres surrounded by red edges on upper body, green stripe from above eye along back to tail base, pale belly and two ocelli on dorsal fin. Juveniles black with yellow stripes along body and two large blue centred ocelli on dorsal fin.

Green-brown with a broad light stripe from corner of mouth, above pectoral fin base to tail, a small black spot at base of dorsal fin in front of tail base. Oblique reddish blotches above stripe present in larger individuals. Dark borders on stripe which diffuse to spots towards tail, and another small black spot on dorsal fin in smaller individuals.
Adults with pointed head, purple face grading to yellow tail, dorsal fin with black patch at front, white pelvic fins. Juveniles white with black stripes from snout to tail.

Males green with blue chain like stripes along body, blue margins on dorsal, tail and anal fins and blue-edged red stripes on face. Juveniles with an ocellus mid way along dorsal fin and a second ocellus on upper tail base. Females and juveniles with yellow and blue stripes along body similar to H. melanurus (Hoeven's Wrasse), best distinguished by presence of males.

White elongate body, with a single lateral stripe from snout to upper tail base, varying in colour from light yellow, pink, to black and zigzagging up and down one scale width. Lacks tail base spot of H. trimaculatus (Threespot Wrasse).

photos.photographer: Cano Tsang; 114°E Hong Kong Reef Fish Survey
Yiu Wai Hong; 114°E Hong Kong Reef Fish Survey
Marco Chan; 114°E Hong Kong Reef Fish Survey

description: Pale body with black spot on upper tail base, smaller black spot behind operculum, pink lines on face breaking into spots behind head, yellow tail. Younger individuals lack spot behind operculum and yellow tail, have less distinct facial markings and may have a yellow instead of black spot on tail base. Lacks horizontal stripe of H. scapularis (Zigzag Wrasse), but lives in similar sandy and lagoon habitats.

Slightly elongate shell with radial and spiral ridges and is a red-brown colour. The species is common but is often mistaken for juvenile blacklip abalone H. rubra. It remains concealed under rocks during the day.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Small abalone with high spire, small holes, and fine ridges running around the shell. It generally occurs in localised aggregations on rock or individually on Pinna shells that are protruding within seagrass beds.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Smallish abalone with numerous distinctive spiral ridges and a more elongate shell than other local species. It is extremely cryptic, dwelling in caves and under rock slabs, mainly on limestone reefs, and is one of the rarer abalone species.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Smooth light-coloured shell, green tentacles and green edge to the foot. The species prefers more sheltered conditions than the other large abalone, and congregates on the edge of reefs and boulders near sand or seagrass beds.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Endemic to South Africa. The largest and most abundant abalone species in this area.

photos.location: Cape Town, Western Cape Province, South Africa
Cape Town, Western Cape Province, South Africa

description: Numerous fine ridges, but lacks the diffuse outward-radiating ribs of most other abalone. It is most abundant at low-tide level in wave-swept areas, with the shells of animals in the most exposed locations often heavily eroded. The species naturally occurs in extremely high densities on limestone rock platforms near Perth and is exploited by both commercial and recreational fishers. It is able to occur in such high densities only because it does not rely on the limited food growing in the immediate vicinity, but feeds mainly on drifting macroalgae.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Large reddish abalone with a black-edged foot and numerous fine spiral ridges around the shell that are crossed by irregular radiating ribs. The shells on larger animals are often heavily eroded and partly covered by algae and sessile animals. Although animals tend to aggregate in crevices, this is also the most conspicuous of the large gastropods on most shallow southeastern Australian reefs. Some authorities consider southwestern animals to be a separate species, Haliotis conicopora, because they grow to a larger size than eastern animals and have a darker and less obviously ribbed shell.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Wide spiral ridge running around the shell between the row of holes and the spire. This ridge is best seen on the inside of the shell, where it forms an obvious groove. The internal groove of animals east of central South Australia is not as sharply cornered as in western animals, and the eastern animals were called H. emmae until recently. Haliotis scalaris resembles H. rubra, but is a smaller animal and has a wide groove around the outside of the shell next to the row of holes.
editor_name: GJ Edgar. 2008. Australian Marine Life. New Holland, Sydney

description: Oblong ovular shell, with a low profile and a row of green ringed holes towards outer edge. Endemic to South Africa.

photos.location: Cape Town, Western Cape Province, South Africa
Cape Town, Western Cape Province, South Africa

description: Transulcent white to pink nudibranch found on the sponge Halisarca laxus which is found on a stalked ascidian Pyura.

Reddish to brown with pale blotches over body and tail, and tassles over face and body. One of a few Batrachoidid frogfishes encountered by divers searching crevices of reefs, but easily missed. Wounds from venomous spines are very painful.
Iridescent blue lines on the body and blue rings on the arms which brighten and flash when disturbed.

Characteristic neon blue rings that glow strongly when the animal is irritated, but they are quite pale when the animal is resting and therefore may not be immediately apparent. The blue-ringed octopus is one of the more infamous sea creatures because of the powerful nerve toxin that is injected with saliva if the animal is strongly provoked and bites. Despite its reputation, the species is not usually aggressive, remaining hidden among broken rock and shell during the day and venturing out from these refuges to feed at night. The female lays about 50 eggs in late autumn and carries them around under her arms for about six months. Once the eggs have hatched, the female dies. Young rapidly grow to maturity and mate in early autumn. The males then die, and the females continue on with the eggs.
